passage:
Librarian's note, Friday
For two weeks Maria has spent every lunch at the back table, where she used to sit with Pallavi and three others. The others eat in the canteen now; Pallavi walks past the library window without looking in. A classmate of Maria's showed me, worried, that her status says "some people show you who they are 🙂", a smile that doesn't look like one. Meanwhile she has signed up for debate, quiz and the eco club, all in one week, and was here till six on Wednesday. Today I asked if she would help me shelve returns. Halfway through the history section she said, very fast, "We were five and now I'm one," and cried into the atlas cart. I sat with her until the bell. She said she hadn't told her parents because "it's just friends". I told her it's allowed to hurt like this, and with her agreement I phoned her mother after school. Her mother is coming in on Monday; Maria has asked to keep shelving on Tuesdays.

qa.q: Who used to sit at the back table with Maria?
qa.a: Pallavi and three others used to sit there with Maria.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she said 'We were five and now I'm one'?
qa.a: Maria felt heartbroken and lonely after the group split, crying into the atlas cart; the rush of new clubs may also show she was trying to outrun the sadness.

qa.q: How did the librarian support Maria?
qa.a: The librarian gave Maria a quiet task, sat with her through the tears, said it was allowed to hurt, and with her agreement brought in her mother.

qa.q: What might the classmate who showed the status have been feeling?
qa.a: That classmate was likely worried about Maria, reading a smiley under a sad line as a sign she wasn't okay, and chose to tell an adult.

grounding: It shows a teenager after a friend-group split withdrawing, posting a cryptic status and piling on activities, and a caring adult helping bring in family support.

passage: At the sports club, Anand had always been the loudest person on the badminton court, commentating on his own smashes. This week he hit quietly, missed easy shuttles and sat on the bench between games staring at his laces. Sharmila noticed he hadn't made a single joke in three sessions. She thought about guessing: a fight at home? Exams? Instead, at the water tap, she said, "You've been really quiet. How are you, really?" Anand shrugged, then said, "My grandfather's in hospital. I've been sleeping on the corridor bench to give Mum a break. I'm just tired." Sharmila didn't offer a pep talk. "That sounds so hard. Do you want me to tell Coach, so you're not in trouble for missing drills?" He hesitated, then nodded. Coach Mehra came over, sat on the bench beside him and said, "Train when you can. Rest is training too. Tell me what you need."

qa.q: Where has Anand been sleeping?
qa.a: Anand has been sleeping on the corridor bench at the hospital.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Anand stopped joking?
qa.a: Sharmila felt curious and a bit worried, tempted to guess at a fight or exams, but chose to ask instead of deciding.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila asked a gentle 'How are you, really?' instead of guessing, listened without a pep talk, and with Anand's agreement brought in Coach, who offered flexibility.

qa.q: What was the week like for Anand?
qa.a: Anand was exhausted and worried about his grandfather, sleeping in the corridor, so he had no energy left for jokes or drills.

grounding: It shows a teenager noticing a peer being quiet and tired, asking gently rather than guessing, and involving a trusted adult.

passage:
Thursday
Group project meeting in the library. I suggested we make the model from recycled cardboard instead of buying thermocol, and Vasudha did the thing. Eyes rolled up to the ceiling, lip curled on one side, and a slow "cuuute" like I was a toddler showing her a drawing. Two others laughed. It's not the first time. My face went hot and my first thought was something nasty about her handwriting. Instead I waited a breath and said, as flat as I could, "When you roll your eyes and say cute, it feels like you think I'm stupid. I'd like to finish the idea." The table went quiet. Vasudha said, "God, relax," but she didn't interrupt again. I finished. We're using cardboard. Mona leaned over afterwards: "Ritu, that was so calm." I didn't feel calm. I felt shaky. If it keeps happening, I'll ask Ma'am to switch me to another group.

qa.q: What did Ritu suggest making the model from?
qa.a: Ritu suggested making it from recycled cardboard instead of buying thermocol.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when Vasudha said 'cuuute'?
qa.a: Ritu felt hurt and belittled, face hot, and angry enough to want to say something nasty; the eye-roll and curled lip read as contempt, though Vasudha may also have been playing to the others.

qa.q: Why did naming the effect work better than a nasty comeback?
qa.a: Calmly saying how the eye-roll landed and asking to finish kept Ritu's dignity, stopped the interruptions and got the idea heard without a fight. 👍

qa.q: How might the two who laughed have been affected by Ritu's response?
qa.a: The table went quiet, so they may have realised the laugh was at someone's expense and felt awkward about joining in.

grounding: It shows a teenager recognising an eye-roll, curled lip and dismissive tone as contempt, and responding by calmly naming the effect, with leaving as the next option.

subtype: Defiant, irritated and frustrated with authority [Mismatch]
passage: In Class 11 I once told Varun Sir, in front of everyone, "Why should I? Give me detention, I don't care." He had asked me to read my answer aloud. I remember crossing my arms and staring at the fan while thirty people went "ooooh". What nobody knew was that I'd been up till two every night that week helping at my uncle's dhaba after my father's accident, and I hadn't written any answer at all. Reading aloud would have shown that. Varun Sir didn't write me up. He said, "Stay back after class, Akash." I expected a lecture. Instead he asked, "Is this about the reading, or about something else?" I nearly said nothing again. Then it all came out: the dhaba, the hospital, the no sleep. He moved my deadline and, with my permission, told the school counsellor I needed some flexibility. I stopped backtalking him after that. Not because I was scared. Because he'd asked.

qa.q: What had Varun Sir asked Akash to do?
qa.a: He had asked Akash to read the answer aloud.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when saying 'Give me detention, I don't care'?
qa.a: Akash was exhausted and afraid of being exposed for not writing anything, and the defiance covered that; there may also have been anger about everything happening at home.

qa.q: What made Varun Sir's response effective?
qa.a: He didn't punish on the spot but asked after class whether it was about the reading or something else, then moved the deadline and, with permission, told the counsellor.

qa.q: How might the class have read Akash's refusal?
qa.a: The thirty classmates going 'ooooh' likely saw plain rebellion, not the tiredness and fear behind it.

grounding: It shows a teenager's backtalk and refusal hiding exhaustion and fear, and an adult who asks before punishing learning the real reason.

passage: The power had been out in the hostel for three hours, the inverter was dying, and Ankita's online mock test started at nine. She reached for her charger. It wasn't there. "Dolma. Where's my charger?" Dolma looked up from her bed, guilty. "I took it to the library... I think I left it there." Something white-hot shot up Ankita's neck. "You THINK? My test is at nine! You always do this!" She slammed the cupboard so hard the mirror rattled. Dolma shrank against the wall. Ankita opened her mouth for more, then heard her own voice echoing down the corridor. She grabbed her dupatta and walked out, down three flights, into the drizzle. She stood under the cycle shed breathing slowly, counting drops off the tin roof, until her hands stopped shaking. Twenty minutes later she went back. Dolma had borrowed a charger from the warden. "I'm sorry I shouted," Ankita said. "I'm still annoyed. But I'm sorry."

qa.q: When did Ankita's online mock test start?
qa.a: It started at nine.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she slammed the cupboard?
qa.a: Ankita was furious and panicky about the test with a dying inverter; 'You always do this' suggests older frustration was spilling out too.

qa.q: What helped Ankita's fury fade without more damage?
qa.a: She noticed her own voice, walked away, breathed slowly under the shed and came back twenty minutes later to apologise.

qa.q: What was it like for Dolma when Ankita shouted?
qa.a: Dolma felt guilty and a bit frightened, shrinking against the wall, and tried to make it right by borrowing a charger from the warden.

grounding: It shows a teenager's fury peaking in shouting and a slammed cupboard, then fading as she steps away, breathes and returns to talk.

passage:
Sahil: Ravi was glaring at me all through PE
Sahil: then he stood in the corridor door and wouldn't let me pass. said "watch yourself after school"
Deepak: wait what. did he touch you?
Sahil: no. just blocked me and did that sneer thing. my legs are still shaky tbh
Deepak: ok. don't go back at him. not worth it
Sahil: part of me wants to. he's done this to 3 people
Deepak: that's exactly why. stay where people are. where are you now?
Sahil: canteen
Deepak: stay there, I'm coming. then we go to Mr Khan together before last bell
Sahil: ok
(40 minutes later)
Sahil: told Mr Khan. he wrote everything down, he's calling Ravi's parents today and he'll walk me to the bus himself
Deepak: good. I'll wait at the bus stop with you too

qa.q: What did Ravi say in the corridor?
qa.a: Ravi said "watch yourself after school".

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling after being blocked in the corridor?
qa.a: Sahil felt scared, legs still shaky, and also angry enough to want to hit back; the glaring and blocking felt like a real threat.

qa.q: Which steps kept Sahil safer?
qa.a: Not retaliating, staying in the busy canteen, going with Deepak to Mr Khan before last bell, and Mr Khan acting that day by calling Ravi's parents and walking Sahil to the bus.

qa.q: How did Deepak read the situation?
qa.a: Deepak saw Ravi's behaviour as a warning sign rather than a challenge, and wanted Sahil safe among people with an adult involved quickly.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading glaring, sneering and blocking as hostility, and responding by disengaging, staying near others and involving a trusted adult.

subtype: Apologetic and pleading in peer conflict [Interpreting]
passage: Three days after Urmila told half the hostel floor about Lakshmi's crush, the apologies began. Seven messages in one night: sorry sorry SORRY, please talk to me, I can't sleep. At breakfast in the mess Urmila slid into the seat opposite, voice soft and wobbly. "I've said sorry like a hundred times. What more do you want?" Lakshmi stirred her upma. The sorry sounded real. It also sounded like a deadline. Later Lakshmi went to the warden's office. "Mrs Joseph, how do I know if she means it?" The warden thought. "Not from how many times she says it. Watch what she does over the next few weeks. And you're allowed to say you need time." That evening Lakshmi replied: "I believe you're sorry. I need some time before we're close again." Urmila left her alone for a week. Then, in the common room, she stood up for Lakshmi when someone else brought the crush up.

qa.q: How many messages did Urmila send in one night?
qa.a: Urmila sent seven messages in one night.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling as she stirred her upma?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt torn and wary: the sorry sounded real, but 'What more do you want?' felt like pressure, and she was still hurt about the crush being spread.

qa.q: How did Mrs Joseph's advice help?
qa.a: It moved the test from how often Urmila says sorry to what she does over the next weeks, and gave Lakshmi permission to take time.

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling while sending seven messages?
qa.a: Urmila was probably guilty and anxious to fix things fast, which made the apology come out as pressure; giving space and later defending Lakshmi showed the sorry becoming real.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a peer's pleading apologies, judging sincerity by changed behaviour over time, and keeping the boundary of needing time.

passage:
"Lavanya, why is your door locked?"
"Go away, Amma."
"Your Paati's reading glasses are in two pieces under the sofa."
Silence.
"Lavanya?"
"I sat on them. This morning. I hid them there." Her voice cracked. "I'm such a horrible person. I ruin everything."
Usha sat down on the floor outside the door. "Okay. Two different things just came out. You broke Paati's glasses and hid them. That was a bad thing to do. Is that what you mean?"
"I mean I'm bad."
"That part I don't accept. A bad thing happened. You're my daughter, and you're not bad."
The lock clicked. Lavanya's face was blotchy. "She can't read her newspaper."
"No. So what could fix that?"
"...I could use my birthday money for new ones. And say sorry. And read her the paper till they come."
"That sounds like someone who cares, not someone who's bad."
"Will you come with me when I tell her?"
"Right behind you."

qa.q: Where were Paati's glasses hidden?
qa.a: The glasses were in two pieces under the sofa.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling behind the locked door?
qa.a: Lavanya felt deep shame, saying 'I'm bad' and hiding, not just guilt about the glasses; there may also have been fear of Paati's reaction.

qa.q: How did Usha help turn shame into repair?
qa.a: Usha separated the act from the person, 'A bad thing happened... you're not bad', then asked what could fix it, so Lavanya came up with sorry, new glasses and reading the paper.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had said 'How could you be so careless?'
qa.a: Lavanya would likely have hidden further behind the door, feeling confirmed as bad, instead of moving towards repair.

grounding: It shows a teenager's 'I am bad' shame and 'I did something bad' guilt looking alike from outside, and a parent responding to the person with care so repair can follow.

passage:
"Everyone's looking at me," Jagdish muttered, tugging his kurta collar.
"Nobody's looking at you," Urmila-didi said. "They're looking at the paneer counter."
"My face is red. I can feel it."
"It's a wedding in May. Everyone's red. This shamiana is an oven."
"I'll just sit in the car."
"You sat in the car at the last three functions. Try one small thing. Just one. Then the car, if you want."
"Like what?"
"Say hi to Mani Mama. He's alone at the juice table. He loves trains. You don't even have to talk much. Just ask about a train."
Jagdish looked at the juice table as if it were a cliff edge. "And if I say something stupid?"
"Then he'll talk about trains anyway."
He took a breath and walked over. Four minutes later he was holding a sugarcane juice and nodding while Mani Mama drew a route map on a napkin. He glanced back and rolled his eyes, but he stayed.
"Car?" she mouthed.
He shook his head. "Later."

qa.q: Who was alone at the juice table?
qa.a: Mani Mama was alone at the juice table.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he tugged his collar?
qa.a: Jagdish felt self-conscious and embarrassed, sure everyone was looking at his red face; there was also worry about saying something stupid.

qa.q: Why was Urmila-didi's 'one small thing' a good suggestion?
qa.a: It gave Jagdish a tiny, safe step, one question about trains with a way out afterwards, which built comfort instead of pushing him into the crowd. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mani Mama have felt when Jagdish came over?
qa.a: Mani Mama, alone at the table, was probably pleased to have company, happily drawing a route map on a napkin.

grounding: It shows a teenager's blushing and self-consciousness at a family function, and a small step into conversation building comfort.

passage:
Tutor's note, Saturday batch
While I explained the trigonometry identities, Eshaan sat sideways, nodding, eyes flicking to the phone under his desk every half minute. Himani sat straight, pen ready, looking right at me. I was sure I knew which of them was listening. Rather than take the phone, I asked each of them one quick question. Eshaan answered his perfectly and added, a bit sheepishly, that he was watching for a message because his mother was at the hospital for his sister's scan and had promised to text. Himani went pink and admitted she had followed the first part but lost track and was too embarrassed to say. So both my guesses were wrong. I told Eshaan he could keep the phone face up on the desk today, and after class I went over the second half with Himani. From next week I'll do a two-question check halfway through, for everyone.

qa.q: Why was Eshaan watching his phone?
qa.a: His mother was at the hospital for his sister's scan and had promised to text.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she went pink?
qa.a: Himani felt embarrassed at having lost track after the first part, which her attentive posture had hidden; there may also have been relief at getting help after class.

qa.q: What did the tutor learn, and what will change?
qa.a: The tutor learned that posture didn't show who was listening, and will add a quick two-question check halfway through for everyone instead of guessing.

qa.q: What would have changed if the tutor had taken Eshaan's phone?
qa.a: Eshaan might have missed news about his sister's scan and felt unfairly punished, even though he was actually following.

grounding: It shows a teenager who looks distracted actually listening and one who looks attentive being lost, and a brief question checking attention better than posture.
